routes.description: Establish that contingent reality requires an explanation outside the totality of contingent things, that this explanatory foundation exists necessarily, and that its comparative explanatory virtues support identifying it as God.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if contingency remains distinct from causal determination, the explanatory principle applies to the plurality of contingent things without an illicit composition inference, and a perfect necessary being is supported over a necessary-universe terminus.

motionBridge.description: Connect the necessary foundation of contingent reality to God through a warranted deductive or abductive identification.

centralBridges.description: Establish that reality includes genuinely contingent things whose existence calls for explanation despite any deterministic causal history.
Show that explaining contingent things individually or through their plurality does not remove the need for a non-contingent explanatory foundation.
Show that simplicity, absence of arbitrary limits, or cumulative theistic considerations favor a perfect necessary being over a necessary universe.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify the relationship between modal contingency, existential dependence, causal determination, and explanatory need.
Ground the demand for explanation in ordinary inquiry, scientific practice, induction, or the stable order of reality.

routes.description: Block the theistic contingency inference by challenging the establishment of genuine contingency, the move from contingent members to an external foundation, and the identification of any necessary reality as God rather than the universe.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if determinism or a necessary-universe option remains viable, if the totality-level explanatory demand is unsupported, or if the proposed divine terminus lacks a non-question-begging advantage over non-theistic necessary reality.

motionBridge.description: Show that the argument does not establish a distinct necessary foundation with attributes sufficient for identification as God.

centralBridges.description: Require justification that observed things could have existed differently and test whether determinism transmits necessity through the causal order.
Show that moving from explanations of contingent members to an explanation outside their totality may assume composition or explanatory convergence.
Preserve a necessary or brute universe as an alternative explanatory terminus and test whether it is at least as simple as a divine foundation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require a principled distinction between treating God as necessarily self-explanatory and allowing comparable treatment of non-divine reality.
Examine whether perfection, unlimited power, divine will, or theological complexity supports rather than undermines the claimed identification.

sections.title: Contingency, Determinism, and Necessity
sections.rationale: The first-stage argument depends on whether anything is genuinely contingent and whether causal determination differs from metaphysical necessity or instead transmits necessity through the causal chain.

sections.title: Explanatory Principle and Legitimate Stopping Points
sections.rationale: The competing burdens require determining why contingent existence calls for explanation and whether explanatory termination at God is principled when analogous termination at non-divine reality is proposed.

sections.title: Plurality, Composition, and External Explanation
sections.rationale: The central transition from explanations of individual contingent things to an explanation beyond their totality turns on composition, plurality, regress, convergence, and possible circularity concerns.

sections.title: Necessary Being or Necessary Universe
sections.rationale: Even if some necessary reality is granted, the motion requires comparison between a distinct necessary being and the option that the universe or lawful reality is itself necessary or brute.

sections.title: Identification with God and Explanatory Virtues
sections.rationale: The final motion-level inference requires grounds for divine attributes and tests whether perfection, simplicity, absence of arbitrary limits, and cumulative theistic considerations distinguish God from rival foundations.

moves.speaker: Cameron Bertuzzi
moves.proposition: If reality has a necessary part and that necessary part is God, the first-stage conclusion combines with this identification to entail that God exists.
moves.attributionBasis: The host asks for the second stage, and Cameron immediately states its premise and resulting conclusion in a continuous turn.

response.rationale: This constructive move states the second-stage conditional linking a necessary part identified as God to the conclusion that God exists.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states the intended motion-level bridge but does not independently defend its identifying premise.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted entailment is properly conditional: if the identifying premise holds, the stated conclusion follows.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The argument must justify that apparently contingent things genuinely could have existed differently, because determinism may eliminate the modal alternatives required to classify them as contingent.

components.text: Challenges the required first-stage assumption that reality contains genuinely contingent things.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a decisive presupposition but does not directly address the target move's separate identification of necessity with God.

charity.alternative: Contingency may concern dependence rather than only alternative possible histories.
charity.decisiveQualification: The presented argument still needs to specify and justify the operative notion of contingency.

moves.speaker: Cameron Bertuzzi
moves.proposition: A result can be causally determined without existing necessarily, because the determining system and its existence can still require explanation.
moves.attributionBasis: The host directly requests Cameron's response, and Cameron supplies the gumball-machine illustration in an uninterrupted answer.

components.text: Identifies the objection's conflation of causal determination with metaphysical necessity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The counterexample only needs to show that determination does not by itself establish necessity, which it does.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central challenge to genuine contingency by separating determination from necessity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts a determined red-ball output with the still-open question why the machine and its arrangement exist.

moves.speaker: Cameron Bertuzzi
moves.proposition: Ordinary inquiry, scientific explanatory practice, inductive generalization, and the stable order of reality jointly support seeking explanations for contingent existence.

components.text: The modal demand to establish that apparently contingent things could have been otherwise.

moves.speaker: Cameron Bertuzzi
moves.proposition: Modal contingency, understood as the capacity to fail to exist, differs from existential dependence, though both notions can contribute to a contingency argument.
moves.attributionBasis: Cameron directly answers Alex's terminology question and explicitly names and explains the distinction between contingency and dependence.

components.text: Replaces an exclusively modal demand with a distinction between possible nonexistence and existential dependence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents a useful distinction rather than claiming that dependence alone completes the contingency argument.

charity.decisiveQualification: Clarifying dependence does not itself prove the modal premise originally demanded.

moves.speaker: Cameron Bertuzzi
moves.proposition: Saying that a thing exists because it was determined to exist is circular if it leaves unexplained why the thing or determining arrangement exists.
moves.attributionBasis: The host explicitly turns back to Cameron, who restates and extends his gumball-machine response until Alex interrupts with a challenge.

components.text: Rejects determination as sufficient to explain why the determined thing or arrangement exists.

response.rationale: The response contacts the explanatory use of determinism but only partially answers the target because it leaves the requested modal proof unresolved.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a decisive explanatory component while leaving the distinct modal-alternative demand unanswered.

charity.alternative: A deterministic explanation may cite laws and antecedent conditions rather than merely repeat that the thing exists.
charity.decisiveQualification: That richer causal explanation can still leave the existence of the laws and conditions unexplained.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: If God's existence may be explained internally or treated as brute necessity, an equivalent explanatory stopping point must remain available for some non-divine reality unless a relevant difference is established.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex explicitly interrupts Cameron and poses a focused first-person challenge contrasting the treatment of God with the treatment of other entities.

components.text: Demands a relevant distinction between God's stopping point and comparable non-divine stopping points.
Questions whether necessary existence alone warrants identifying the terminus as God.

response.rationale: The objection directly challenges the asymmetry between rejecting brute or internal explanation elsewhere and permitting it for God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive stopping-point premise and states the consequence if no relevant difference is supplied.

precisionFindings.rationale: The symmetry demand is clear, though describing a necessary being as its own cause blurs causation and necessary self-explanation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately poses a parity challenge rather than claiming that every entity is actually self-explanatory.

charity.alternative: God may be necessarily existent without being self-caused, unlike contingent physical things.
charity.decisiveQualification: A principled difference still must be established rather than assumed through terminology.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The symmetry challenge is strong, with a bounded ambiguity between self-causation, self-explanation, and brute necessity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the subsidiary burden of pressing principled stopping-point symmetry.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection reaches the strongest parity issue but partially conflates necessary existence with self-causation.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: If a necessary foundation necessarily produces the causal chain, necessity propagates through its effects, so every subsequent event in the universe occurs necessarily rather than contingently.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly addresses Alex at the end of the uninterrupted objection, while Cameron begins his answer on the following row.

components.text: Introduces the stronger case where a necessary antecedent necessarily produces each subsequent effect.
Argues that the complete necessary chain removes contingency rather than merely explaining an outcome.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the prior distinction with a stronger modal premise, though that premise itself remains undefended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional necessity-transmission claim is recoverable and consistently scoped to necessary production.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The inference works if each production relation is necessary, but the move does not establish that a necessary foundation must act necessarily.

charity.alternative: A necessary foundation could contingently exercise causal power or will among multiple possible effects.
charity.decisiveQualification: Necessity transmits only if the causal relation and antecedent conditions are themselves necessary.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Necessity transmission is valid under the stated necessary-production condition, but that central condition is not independently supported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The causal-chain illustration clarifies the claim, while leaving the modal status of the causal laws and divine action asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central challenge to genuine contingency through a necessity-transmission argument.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt traces a supposedly necessary cause through the hand, machine, lever, and resulting gumball output.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Rejecting self-causation as absurd does not support the argument unless the allegedly self-explanatory necessary existence of God is relevantly distinguished from the structure rejected elsewhere.
moves.attributionBasis: The first-person objection follows Cameron's self-causation argument and ends immediately before Cameron explicitly answers from his own conception of God.

components.text: Challenges consistency between rejecting self-causation and allowing God to terminate explanation.
Argues that labeling God non-contingent does not by itself exempt God from explanatory scrutiny.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the proposed explanatory stopping point and demands a distinction between absurd self-causation and necessary self-explanation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly reaches the consistency issue, although its own wording partly conflates self-causation with necessary existence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The consistency demand is clear, but 'self cause for God' is not stably distinguished from uncaused necessary existence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: God would require another explanation only if necessary existence lacks the relevant distinction; that conditional qualification is compressed.

charity.alternative: The theist may regard God as uncaused and necessarily existent, not self-caused.
charity.decisiveQualification: The theist must still warrant why necessary existence is coherent and explanatorily sufficient.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parity concern is coherent, but the conflation of self-causation with necessary uncaused existence materially weakens the inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument exposes a needed distinction, yet its conclusion depends heavily on an inadequately defended conceptual equivalence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the subsidiary stopping-point burden by testing consistency in explanatory termination.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection identifies a legitimate consistency burden but materially weakens the view by recasting uncaused necessity as self-causation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that if self-causation is absurd for non-contingent beings, treating God similarly would require another explanation.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The explanatory needs of individual contingent members do not by themselves establish that their complete collection requires a further explanation, because that inference risks a fallacy of composition.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained objection uses Alex's first-person framing and is followed by the moderator expressly inviting Cameron to answer it.

components.text: Challenges the move from explanations of each contingent member to explanation of the complete collection.
Questions whether a further totality-level explanation is required once members are explained.

response.rationale: The objection directly identifies the composition bridge that must be defended before individual explanatory needs support a totality-level demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive totality inference and carefully notes that composition risk is not automatic falsity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The member-to-collection inference is precisely identified, and the objection explicitly avoids treating the fallacy label as decisive.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move properly claims a risk requiring further warrant, not that every collection inference is necessarily fallacious.

charity.alternative: Some properties, including contingency or unexplained existence, may legitimately transfer to a plurality.
charity.decisiveQualification: The transfer still requires an argument tailored to explanation rather than mere aggregation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The objection clearly isolates the member-to-totality inference and accurately treats composition as a warrant demand rather than a label.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual support is specific and representative, with only a fuller comparison of legitimate totality inferences omitted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central bridge from contingent members to a further explanation of their totality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection expressly grants that a composition concern need not make the conclusion false and targets only the missing bridge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks whether every member requiring explanation entails that the group itself requires an explanation and qualifies the fallacy charge.

moves.speaker: Cameron Bertuzzi
moves.proposition: Considering contingent things as a plurality avoids treating them as a further composed object, while separate explanations of every member still leave why that plurality exists unanswered.
moves.attributionBasis: Cameron is explicitly given the floor before the response, and Alex begins his contrary answer on the immediately following row.

components.text: Recasts all contingent things as a plurality rather than an additional composed object.
Argues that member-level explanations leave why this plurality exists unanswered.

response.rationale: The reply contacts both the composition diagnosis and the residual explanatory demand by denying an extra whole while retaining a plurality-level question.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly addresses the decisive composition concern and supplies a concrete factory illustration of the residual question.

precisionFindings.rationale: Plurality is consistently distinguished from a composed object, and the residual question is clearly scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The illustration shows an unanswered question but does not fully establish that every complete member explanation must omit a plurality explanation.

charity.alternative: A complete set of member explanations might jointly explain why exactly those members exist without an extra collective cause.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must show why such distributed explanations cannot collectively answer the plurality question.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt uses the camera-factory case to argue that explaining each camera still leaves why cameras, or any cameras, exist.

moves.proposition: The camera-factory illustration does not establish a single external necessary source, because it either presupposes that separate explanatory chains converge on one source or permits them not to converge.
moves.attributionBasis: The row begins an explicit objection to Cameron's factory example, and the moderator takes over directly after the argument concludes.

components.text: Challenges the assumption that distinct member explanations converge upon one external source.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: If determinism means there are no genuinely contingent things, the universe may itself be necessary and therefore need no additional necessary being beyond it as an explanation.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage answers the moderator's necessary-universe question in Alex's first-person voice, after which the moderator explicitly requests Cameron's response.

components.text: Offers the universe itself as a necessary terminus if genuine contingency has not been established.

moves.proposition: Labeling the necessary part of reality God does not establish a distinct perfect being, because the connection between necessary existence, perfection, and substantive divine attributes still requires argument.

moves.speaker: Cameron Bertuzzi
moves.proposition: A perfect being avoids the unexplained arbitrary limits that would arise if a necessary foundation possessed only a particular finite degree of creative power.
moves.attributionBasis: This is a numbered continuation of Cameron's uninterrupted response, framed as his third explanatory virtue of a perfect being.

components.text: Claims that a perfect being avoids arbitrary finite limits afflicting rival necessary foundations.

response.rationale: The reply supplies another comparative virtue by arguing that finite foundational powers introduce unexplained limit facts absent from perfection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the comparative demand with a concrete consideration, though it does not show that the universe rival has the posited finite power.

precisionFindings.rationale: The arbitrary-limit objection is clear, but its application shifts between a foundation within the universe and the universe hypothesis generally.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Specific finite limits can invite explanation, but unlimited perfection may also require substantive coherence and does not automatically win.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: A brute universe governed by simple mathematical laws may be simpler than a willing God, whose will introduces further contingency and dependence questions rather than improving explanatory economy.
moves.attributionBasis: The move continues Alex's allocated response and develops a distinct universe-based alternative to Cameron's perfect-being explanation.

components.text: Counters that simple mathematical laws may be less complex than a God possessing a will.

response.rationale: The response directly contests the claimed simplicity advantage and supplies a concrete source of possible divine complexity: will and its modal dependence.

moves.speaker: Cameron Bertuzzi
moves.proposition: The plurality of all contingent things cannot explain itself, so its explanation must lie outside that plurality in a non-contingent and therefore necessary being.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly asks Cameron for his conclusion, and the answer restates the staged contingency argument from contingent things to a necessary being.

response.rationale: This constructive conclusion assembles the plurality argument: self-explanation is rejected, so the explanation is placed outside contingent reality in a necessary being.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it explicitly supplies the central external-foundation inference, though key exclusion premises remain compressed.
